research.summary:
BOTTOM LINE: For this project, merging drone (aerial) images and Insta360 ground images into ONE splat (option b) costs a lot and gains little. Use it only as an optional experiment. The evidence-based choice: (a) LiDAR + Insta360 for the first test, then (c) the drone as a separate aerial layer registered into the shared (LiDAR) frame as a later optional phase. Nothing found argues for bringing the drone forward.

1) WHAT THE LITERATURE SHOWS. Most aerial+ground radiance-field papers are urban, often synthetic, and run on A100-class GPUs.
- MatrixCity (ICCV 2023): naive aerial+street fusion degraded NeRFs badly (Mip-NeRF360 aerial PSNR 28.37 -> 17.07; TensoRF 27.26 -> 21.44).
- Horizon-GS (CVPR 2025, closest state of the art): vanilla 3DGS joint training has "conflicting gradient accumulation". Street views prune occluded Gaussians, aerial views regrow them, and joint training "consistently underperformed separate training". Their fix is two-stage training (aerial gradients first, then street-only densification), camera-sampling balancing (2:1 then 1:1) and multi-LOD. It gives big aerial gains (30.59 vs 28.44 dB vs Scaffold-GS). Street views only reach parity (23.80 vs 23.84 dB). So even the best unified method does not make ground views better than a strong ground-capable baseline; the benefit is one model that renders well from both heights. Real data needed bridging "transitional views", ContextCapture poses, an A100 80 GB and ~4 h/scene. Code is released but under the Inria 3DGS non-commercial license.
- UC-GS (BMVC 2024): with uncertainty-weighted aerial pixels, road views gain only +0.41 to +0.68 dB, on synthetic AirSim/UE data with perfect poses. Naive A+G mainly helped slightly shifted or tilted views.
- Practitioners (heliguy/XGRIDS LCC Aerial-Ground Map Fusion, DJI Terra guides): aerial gives roofs, context and site framework, ground capture gives eye-level detail. Commercial fusion relies on RTK on BOTH devices plus extra ascending bridging shots; others just composite separate splats in SuperSplat. The BLK2GO has no GNSS, so the RTK route is unavailable without GCPs.

2) KNOWN PROBLEMS.
- SfM matching: SIFT degrades past ~30 deg of out-of-plane viewpoint change and keeps >50% accuracy only to ~50 deg on planar scenes. Nadir-vs-horizontal is ~90 deg. DRAGON measured COLMAP registering only 50% of mixed drone+ground images. Learned matchers help in urban scenes: AerialMegaDepth fine-tuning lifts DUSt3R RRA@5 from 5.2% to 56%. Sky2Ground (CVPR 2026) and Aug-2026 detector-free aerial-ground SfM still report hard failures. MASt3R is CC BY-NC-SA; RoMa (MIT) and LightGlue (Apache) are permissive.
- Multi-scale aliasing: needs Mip-style antialiasing (gsplat antialiased=True) or LoD (Octree-GS).
- Appearance/lighting: use per-camera/per-frame compensation. PPISP is in gsplat, Apache, and builds per-camera modules from COLMAP camera ids. Bilateral grid and app_opt are also available.
- Densification imbalance: Horizon-GS-style sampling is not in stock gsplat, so custom code is needed.
- Fixed Gaussian budget on 16 GB: adding aerial content takes Gaussians away from ground detail. gsplat MCMC is 1M = 1.98 GB, 3M = 4.99 GB on Mip-NeRF360. VRAM itself is not the bottleneck at 10x10 m.

3) FOREST-SPECIFIC REASONS MERGING IS WEAK.
- Above-canopy drone images see crown TOPS; ground 360 images see trunks, understory and crown UNDERSIDES against bright sky. Co-visible surfaces are few (edges, gaps), so cross-view matching has little to work with, whatever the matcher.
- In tropical rainforest, gaps are "rare or absent" and SfM usually cannot map the ground (Swinfield 2019). In boreal forest, photogrammetric DEMs are reliable only in open or sparse areas (Brown 2024: RMSE <1.5 m overall, 0.31 m over open terrain).
- Merging also creates an opacity conflict at the canopy layer. Aerial views want opaque canopy-top Gaussians; ground views looking up through gaps want them transparent. This is the Horizon-GS gradient conflict in its worst form. (This is my inference, not a measured result.)
- Moving foliage (wind, rotor downwash) breaks the static-scene assumption most in the canopy. The canopy is also exactly where the drone adds information.
- Resolution: a C0 Mini-class drone (48 MP, 82 deg FOV) at 30 m above the canopy gives ~5 mm/px on crown tops. Insta360 8K equirect gives ~1.6 mm/px at 2 m but ~12 mm/px at 15 m (canopy undersides). The drone therefore resolves the canopy better, but a ground-walk viewer never sees that side.

4) REGISTRATION. With LiDAR present, the shared frame should stay the LiDAR frame.
- Drone imagery would be solved in its own SfM (nadir+oblique grid with EXIF/RTK GNSS priors; COLMAP pose-prior mapper 3.11+) and registered to the BLK2GO cloud. Options: GCP targets in gaps/edges visible from above and in the LiDAR, plus ICP/canopy-shape registration on terrain, trunks at edges and crowns.
- Literature accuracy for aerial-to-ground forest cloud registration is decimetre level: 0.24 m average canopy-shape TLS-ULS; 0.2-0.5 m typical tree-based; 0.05 m northern / 0.17 m tropical for UAV-LiDAR-to-MLS in high-density canopy. Photogrammetric clouds will be worse.
- That error is fine for a separate layer (c) but too coarse for a merged splat (b), which needs roughly pixel-consistent (cm-level) poses near shared surfaces. Option (b) therefore also needs bridging capture plus joint bundle adjustment, or gsplat pose_opt for small residuals.
- When no LiDAR is present, drone GNSS (RTK preferred) defines a georeferenced metric frame. The drone could then be the scale/georef provider for a splat-only project. That is the one scenario where a joint SfM (b-style) has a distinct benefit (inference).

5) VERDICT.
- 10x10 m Swedish plot: (b) is not worth it. Expected ground-view gain ~0 dB, with a real risk of degradation, large SfM/training engineering effort, and NC-licensed reference code. (c) adds canopy-top, terrain context and surroundings for overview and fly-up views at modest cost and with no risk to the ground splat.
- Larger tropical sites: (c) is the only practical option. A closed canopy prevents bridging and the drone sees essentially only the canopy. LoD/chunked aerial training (Octree-GS / CityGaussian class) becomes relevant beyond a few hectares.
- Search budget ran out near the end of this research. Real-data aerial+ground forest splat comparisons and current drone price and regulation details were not searched further.

findings.claim: Naively training one radiance field on aerial + street images degrades quality; this is well documented.
findings.details: MatrixCity (ICCV 2023) Table 5: Mip-NeRF360 aerial PSNR fell from 28.37 to 17.07 after naive fusion, and TensoRF from 27.26 to 21.44. The authors attribute this to the large difference in detail level and in distance to the foreground. In Horizon-GS Fig. 3, joint 3DGS training 'consistently underperformed separate training, even with extensive iterations', and ended with fewer Gaussians.

findings.claim: Even the best unified aerial-to-ground method (Horizon-GS, CVPR 2025) does not improve street-level views over a strong baseline. It mainly improves aerial views and lets one model serve both heights.
findings.details: Horizon-GS Table 1 (small scenes), aerial PSNR/LPIPS: Horizon-GS 30.59/0.094, Scaffold-GS 28.44/0.191, 3D-GS 25.44/0.325. Street PSNR: Horizon-GS 23.80, Scaffold-GS 23.84, Hier-GS 23.75, 3D-GS 21.81. Street SSIM/LPIPS is slightly better at 0.839/0.209 vs 0.819/0.271. Mechanisms: two-stage training (stage 1 uses aerial-only densification gradients with a 2:1 aerial sampling ratio; stage 2 uses street-only gradients at 1:1 with frozen MLPs) and multi-LOD. Ablation: removing camera balancing costs 0.74 dB, densification balancing 0.21 dB, multi-LOD 0.18 dB. Real data used a DJI M350RTK with a 5-camera payload and a 6-camera helmet, 'transitional views' to bridge SfM, and ContextCapture for poses. Images were resized to 1600 px. Ran on an A100 80 GB, ~4 h per large scene.

findings.claim: Where aerial images were shown to improve ground views, the gain was small (+0.4 to +0.7 dB). It came on synthetic urban data with perfect poses and required a specialised training method.
findings.details: UC-GS (BMVC 2024) projects ground-view rendering uncertainty onto aerial images and uses it to weight aerial pixels. Reported gains: +0.68 dB (NYC) and +0.41 dB (SF) PSNR, on a synthetic AirSim/Unreal dataset. The authors state naive A+G training 'does not demonstrate remarkable improvements' on road views and mainly helps slightly shifted or tilted viewpoints (+0.1 m height, -5 deg tilt). Built on Scaffold-GS.

findings.claim: Standard COLMAP/SIFT cannot reliably match nadir drone images to ground-level images (~90 deg viewpoint gap). Bridging images or specialised learned matchers are required, and the matchers are still unreliable.
findings.details: SIFT keeps >50% matching accuracy only up to ~50 deg viewpoint change on planar scenes (Lowe 2004); local features generally fail beyond 25-30 deg of out-of-plane rotation. DRAGON: COLMAP registered only 50.00% of mixed drone+ground views; synthetic intermediate-elevation renders raised this to 97.47%. AerialMegaDepth (CVPR 2025): off-the-shelf DUSt3R RRA@5 on aerial-ground pairs was 5.20%, and 55.96% after fine-tuning. Sky2Ground (CVPR 2026, 51 sites): SkyNet gives +9.6% RRA@5 and +18.1% RTA@5 over MASt3R/VGGT-class methods, and satellite views often degrade results. An Aug-2026 detector-free aerial-ground SfM reports +93.9% AUC@5 vs LoFTR. All of these are urban or landmark scenes, not forests.

findings.claim: Practitioners merging drone and ground data rely on RTK/GCPs and explicit bridging shots rather than pure image matching. Many simply composite separately trained splats.
findings.details: XGRIDS LCC Aerial-Ground Map Fusion requires an RTK fix on both the drone (DJI M4E) and the handheld scanner. The heliguy fusion case used 30 m ortho + 70 m Smart Oblique cross-hatch flights plus manual corner shots ascending at 1 m intervals. Processing took ~5 h on an RTX 5090 with 128 GB RAM. Pix4D recommends 'an informed transition' from nadir to lower-altitude oblique, GCPs or manual tie points, the same lighting, and 85% overlap for oblique sets. DJI Terra-oriented guides recommend compositing a georeferenced aerial splat with ground splats in SuperSplat/SplatForge.

findings.claim: In forests, a drone above the canopy sees mostly crown tops, terrain only in gaps, and essentially no understory. In dense tropical forest it sees almost no ground.
findings.details: Swinfield et al. 2019 (tropical): ground positions are only identified where sufficiently large gaps reach the floor, and these 'can be very rare or absent in dense tropical forests'. SfM has poor penetrability. Brown et al. 2024 (heterogeneous boreal landscape): DEM RMSE was <1.5 m in all cases and as low as 0.31 m over open terrain. Overcast gave the best sparse-forest CHM; clear sky gave the best for the forest class. Terrain reconstruction from images is possible only through gaps or under leaf-off conditions. Inference: in a less dense Swedish pine/spruce plot, expect partial ground visibility in gaps. In closed tropical canopy, expect canopy-only coverage.

findings.claim: In a forest, aerial and ground cameras see mostly different surfaces (crown tops vs. trunks and crown undersides). This weakens both cross-view matching and the benefit of merging, and it creates an opacity conflict at the canopy layer.
findings.details: This is a geometric argument from the evidence above, not a measured result. Ground 360 views look up through the canopy at the sky, so their loss pushes canopy-gap Gaussians toward transparency. Aerial views want opaque canopy-top Gaussians. This is the same 'conflicting gradient accumulation' Horizon-GS describes, concentrated at the canopy. Foliage motion from wind and rotor downwash also breaks the static-scene assumption most in the canopy, which is exactly the region the drone adds.

findings.claim: Registering an above-canopy drone model to a ground/handheld LiDAR cloud without shared GNSS reaches decimetre accuracy. That is enough for a separate layer but not for one merged splat.
findings.details: Canopy-shape TLS-ULS registration: 0.24 m average RMSE (manual 0.18 m); tree-based methods are typically 0.2-0.5 m. A feature-deviation ULS-MLS method gave 0.17 m in tropical plots (canopy density 0.93) and 0.05 m in northern plots (0.75). These figures are for UAV LiDAR, which penetrates the canopy. UAV photogrammetric clouds lack the under-canopy points and should be expected to do worse (inference). A merged splat needs roughly pixel-consistent poses: at 2 m from the Insta360, ~1.6 mm/px.

findings.claim: gsplat (Apache-2.0) already has most of what a careful merge needs: Mip-style antialiasing, per-camera/per-frame appearance (PPISP), bilateral grid, per-image appearance embeddings, pose refinement, MCMC with a hard Gaussian cap, and packed/sparse-grad memory modes. It lacks camera-group sampling weights and stage-wise densification.
findings.details: simple_trainer options include antialiased (default False), app_opt/app_embed_dim=16, post_processing in {bilateral_grid, ppisp}, pose_opt (lr 1e-5), MCMCStrategy cap_max, packed, sparse_grad, depth_loss, masks, and fisheye camera models. PPISP is built as PPISP(num_cameras=parser.num_cameras, num_frames=...), so a drone camera and the Insta360 get separate sensor modules automatically if COLMAP gives them distinct camera ids. 'No explicit image sampling weighting is implemented.' Antialiased mode applies the Mip-Splatting 2D compensation factor. Memory on Mip-NeRF360 (A100): MCMC 1M = 1.98 GB, MCMC 3M = 4.99 GB, default = 5.62 GB. Under a fixed cap, adding aerial content takes Gaussians away from ground detail.

findings.claim: The dedicated aerial-ground and LoD trainers (Horizon-GS, Octree-GS, UC-GS-base Scaffold-GS, Hierarchical-3DGS) are under the Inria 3DGS non-commercial license or have no clear license. They are usable for evaluation, not as production code for a Hexagon tool.
findings.details: Horizon-GS README: 'Please follow the LICENSE of 3D-GS'. Code plus HorizonGS/UCGS/MatrixCity data are released, using a gsplat-based renderer. Octree-GS states the same; it is TPAMI 2025 with MatrixCity support and 2.36 GB memory on MatrixCity vs 3.70 GB. The Inria license allows 'non-commercially, i.e. for research and/or evaluation purposes only'. CityGS-X (ICCV 2025) README shows no license. CityGaussian is reported as CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. LichtFeld Studio is GPLv3 (MCMC, bilateral grid, 3DGUT; CUDA 12.8+, driver 570+).

findings.claim: Forest-specific GS work fusing handheld LiDAR with UAV images exists but is new. I could not verify whether it includes ground-level imagery.
findings.details: 'LiDAR-Guided Semantic 3DGS for Forest Digital Twins' (Remote Sensing 2026) fuses handheld laser point clouds with UAV images using trunk-structure constraints. Reported results: PSNR 24.94 dB, SSIM 0.773, LPIPS 0.231; DBH R² 0.848, RMSE 2.705 cm. The full text was blocked (403), so capture details are unverified. It suggests LiDAR geometry priors help an aerial-image splat in forests.

findings.claim: Scale/GSD mismatch between drone and Insta360 in a forest plot is moderate (~3-10x). That is smaller than in city aerial-street datasets, but it still calls for antialiasing or LoD if both sets of views are rendered from one model.
findings.details: Calculation from specs. DJI Mini 4 Pro: 1/1.3-inch, 8064x6048, 82.1 deg diagonal FOV (~69.6 deg horizontal). At 30 m range the footprint is ~42 m wide: ~5.2 mm/px (48 MP) or ~10.4 mm/px (12 MP binned). Insta360 8K equirect (~7680 px over 360 deg, ~0.82 mrad/px; width assumed): ~1.6 mm/px at 2 m, ~4 mm at 5 m, ~12 mm at 15 m (crown undersides). The drone resolves crown tops 2-3x better than the ground camera resolves crown undersides.

findings.claim: Insta360-incubated Antigravity A1 is a 249 g 8K 360 drone. It could give 360 aerial video from the same camera family, which may ease appearance matching and wide-FOV bridging.
findings.details: Announced Aug 2025, available Dec 2025. Dual-lens 8K 360 video, 1/1.28-inch 55 MP sensor, 24/39 min flight time, GPS/Galileo/BeiDou. The EU class mark and the photogrammetry suitability of stitched 360 drone video are unverified. Dual-lens stitching seams are known to cause SfM misalignment.

recommendations.recommendation: Phase 1: keep option (a), LiDAR + Insta360 only. Do not buy or fly a drone for the first 10x10 m test.
recommendations.rationale: There is no evidence that aerial images improve ground-level views of a forest splat. Horizon-GS only reaches street-view parity, UC-GS gives +0.4-0.7 dB on synthetic data, and naive fusion degrades results. The viewer's main mode is ground navigation, which never sees crown tops. Adding a drone multiplies the SfM, registration and training failure modes before the core LiDAR-splat alignment is proven.
recommendations.alternatives: If an overview image is wanted for the test, a handful of drone photos can be used as documentation only, without integration.

recommendations.recommendation: Later optional phase: implement option (c), the drone as a separate aerial model. Build a drone-only SfM (nadir grid + 4-direction obliques with EXIF/RTK GNSS priors, COLMAP pose-prior mapper) and a drone-only gsplat splat (antialiased=True, PPISP). Register it into the shared frame, which is the LiDAR frame when present. The viewer shows it as its own layer with a camera-height LoD switch or cross-fade at canopy height. Partition the volume using the LiDAR canopy height model, so the ground splat owns everything below the canopy and the aerial splat owns above-canopy surfaces plus surroundings beyond the plot.
recommendations.rationale: It adds canopy-top, terrain and context coverage at modest cost (estimate: days of engineering, 20-30 min of field time). It cannot degrade the ground splat. Decimetre-level registration (0.05-0.25 m in the literature) is acceptable for a separate layer. It also fits the modular source architecture: the drone module emits images, poses, a GNSS frame and a splat layer.
recommendations.alternatives: Use a drone photogrammetric mesh or DSM instead of a splat for the aerial layer (cheaper to stream, LuciadRIA-friendly).

recommendations.recommendation: Treat option (b), one merged splat, as a research experiment only. Attempt it only at an open Swedish site with a forest edge or clearing, with bridging capture and a seamless ground-to-sky fly-up as a hard requirement. Never attempt it in closed tropical canopy.
recommendations.rationale: It needs cm-consistent joint poses, which in turn needs shared co-visible surfaces; a forest has few. It also needs custom trainer changes (camera-group sampling, stage-wise densification) and fights an opacity conflict at the canopy. The reference implementations are licensed non-commercial.
recommendations.alternatives: A 'loose merge': train one gsplat model on ground + drone images, using the poses from (c)'s registration plus gsplat pose_opt. It is cheaper but will likely show ghosting at crown edges and gaps.

recommendations.recommendation: If (b) is attempted, follow this technique: (1) Bridging capture: a descending drone orbit at a gap or edge (e.g. 45-60 deg oblique, stepping down in altitude), ascending shots at plot corners (heliguy used 1 m steps), and Insta360 on a 3-5 m pole. (2) Joint SfM with pose priors and learned matching: ALIKED/LightGlue in COLMAP 4.x or RoMa (MIT). MASt3R or aerial-MASt3R are CC BY-NC-SA and suitable for research only. (3) Separate COLMAP camera ids per sensor, so gsplat PPISP and appearance embeddings separate the drone and Insta360 ISPs. (4) Horizon-GS-style training reimplemented in gsplat: stage 1 aerial-weighted sampling (2:1) with aerial-only densification stats, stage 2 ground-only densification at 1:1. (5) antialiased=True, an MCMC cap of ~3-5M on 16 GB, images downscaled to ~1600 px. (6) Sky masks on ground and oblique images, and operator masks. (7) Gather densification stats from the LiDAR-occupied volume only, or use a LiDAR depth prior.
recommendations.rationale: These are the components that the evidence (Horizon-GS ablations, PPISP, Mip-Splatting/gsplat antialiasing, Pix4D/XGRIDS bridging practice) shows are necessary. They are reimplemented on Apache-licensed code to avoid NC-license exposure.
recommendations.alternatives: Use Horizon-GS code directly, for internal evaluation only (Inria NC license).

recommendations.recommendation: Drone capture protocol, valid for either (b) or (c). Fly the same day as the ground walk, within about ±30 min. Prefer overcast or stable light and low wind. Lock exposure and white balance on both the drone and the Insta360. Shoot 48 MP stills rather than video, using hover-and-shoot or slow speed if the shutter is electronic. Fly a nadir grid plus 4-direction obliques at 30-45 deg off-nadir with ≥80% front and ≥70% side overlap, about 20-30 m above the canopy top. Cover a buffer well beyond the 10x10 m plot (e.g. ~60x60 m) so SfM is well conditioned. Place 3-5 GCP targets in gaps or at edges that are visible from the air, in the BLK2GO cloud and in the Insta360 frames.
recommendations.rationale: Overlap and oblique values come from Pix4D and DJI-workflow guides. The boreal study found overcast best for sparse forest. Foliage motion and lighting changes are the main sources of cross-session inconsistency. GCPs are the only robust bridge because the BLK2GO has no GNSS.
recommendations.alternatives: An RTK drone, either without GCPs (absolute georeferencing) or with them as a check. Inside the plot the LiDAR frame still governs.

recommendations.recommendation: Module design implication: the drone source module should output its own pose set, a GNSS/ENU frame and a splat/mesh layer, plus a registration transform (with an uncertainty estimate) to the shared frame. Joint training with ground images should be an explicit opt-in 'merge' flag, not the default. With no LiDAR, use drone GNSS (RTK preferred) as the georeferenced metric frame. In a drone + Insta360-only project, a joint SfM is the main way the ground splat obtains metric scale.
recommendations.rationale: This keeps (c) as the default path and still allows (b) experiments. It also covers the source-combination matrix the user asked for, including drone-only and drone+splat without LiDAR.
recommendations.alternatives: Scale the drone + Insta360 case with a measured scale bar or GCPs instead of a joint SfM.

tools_and_licenses.notes: Requires RTK on both drone and XGRIDS scanner. Not applicable to a BLK2GO without GNSS. Benchmark of commercial practice only.

risks: Cross-view SfM failure: drone and Insta360 images form disconnected components. In closed canopy this is near-certain, which forces registration through LiDAR, GCPs or GNSS at decimetre accuracy.
Opacity and densification conflict at the canopy layer in a merged splat. Ground views looking up through gaps fight aerial canopy-top Gaussians, giving floaters, holes or haze at crown level.
Under a fixed 16 GB Gaussian budget, merging takes Gaussians away from ground-level detail, which is the viewer's main use case.
Foliage motion from wind and rotor downwash between and during flights breaks the static-scene assumption, mostly in the canopy.
Lighting and appearance mismatch between drone and Insta360 sessions (sun angle, sensor ISP). Mitigated but not eliminated by PPISP or bilateral grids.
License exposure: Horizon-GS, Octree-GS, Hierarchical-3DGS and MASt3R are non-commercial. Using them beyond evaluation inside Hexagon needs legal review.
Registration error of 0.05-0.5 m for drone-to-LiDAR forest alignment shows as visible seams or ghosting if layers are shown simultaneously near the canopy.
The evidence base is mostly urban and synthetic. No peer-reviewed quantitative study of a merged aerial + ground-level splat in forest was found, so expected gains are inferred.
Operational: flying a drone near or under the canopy risks collisions and GNSS loss. Permits and operator registration add lead time (regulatory specifics not verified here).
Web search budget ran out late in this research. Some follow-ups (real-data aerial-ground forest splats, drone pricing, Swedish dissemination-permit status) were not searched.
open_questions: Is there any real-data study of a merged aerial + ground-level splat in forest, with quantitative ground-view metrics? None was found before the search budget ran out.

How well does UAV photogrammetry register to a BLK2GO cloud specifically, given that the BLK2GO sees crowns from below and has ~25 m range? Expect it to be worse than the ULS-MLS figures (0.05-0.17 m).
Does stitched 360 drone video (e.g. Antigravity A1) reconstruct better than a standard drone camera for bridging and appearance consistency with the Insta360?
Exact current status of Swedish aerial-imagery dissemination rules (Lantmäteriet) and the EU class-mark requirements for the candidate drone. These belong to the regulations research topic.
Whether the web viewer (Spark/Three.js or LuciadRIA) can depth-sort two splat layers together for a seamless fly-up, or needs a hard LoD switch.
Whether gsplat's antialiased mode (2D filter only) is enough for ~3-10x scale differences, or a 3D smoothing filter (Mip-Splatting) or LoD is needed.
questions_for_user: Must the viewer support flying above the canopy (bird's-eye or fly-up), or is it primarily a ground-level walkthrough? This decides whether a drone adds any visible value.
Do you have or plan an RTK drone, or GCP targets that can be scanned by the BLK2GO and seen from the air?
Will test sites include a clearing, road or forest edge where drone and ground cameras can see the same surfaces (needed for any merged-splat attempt)?
Is the pipeline for internal R&D only, or could it ship commercially? This determines whether non-commercial reference code (Horizon-GS, Octree-GS, MASt3R) may be used.
Is a drone-only or drone + Insta360 (no LiDAR) mode a real use case, or mainly for completeness? It changes whether the drone must provide the metric or georeferenced frame.

verdicts.claim: MatrixCity (ICCV 2023) shows naive aerial+street fusion degrades quality: Mip-NeRF360 aerial PSNR 28.37 -> 17.07, TensoRF 27.26 -> 21.44.
verdicts.correction: The numbers are right, but the Table 5 caption ('Ablation on the fusion of aerial and street data') does not say which test views the Fusion row is evaluated on, so calling 17.07 the 'aerial PSNR' is an interpretation. The full rows are: Aerial-only 28.37/0.855/0.197, Street-only 23.05/0.805/0.312, Fusion 17.07/0.470/0.600 (Mip-NeRF360); TensoRF 27.26 / 22.10 / 21.44. Fusion is worse than BOTH single-domain models. The authors say 'the ground part of the aerial view becomes dirty after training with the street data' and call for 'finetuning, progressive training, separate group of hyperparameters'. This is 2023 NeRF evidence on synthetic UE city data, not 3DGS. The direction is valid; the evidence is old.

verdicts.claim: Horizon-GS (CVPR 2025) Table 1 small scenes: aerial 30.59/0.094 vs Scaffold-GS 28.44/0.191 and 3D-GS 25.44; street PSNR 23.80 vs Scaffold 23.84, Hier-GS 23.75, 3D-GS 21.81; street SSIM/LPIPS 0.839/0.209 vs 0.819/0.271. Joint 3DGS training 'consistently underperformed separate training'.
verdicts.correction: Also confirmed: Hier-GS street LPIPS is 0.220, and the text says 'with more observed views, the number of final Gaussian primitives are even less'. The large-scale table (Table 2) makes the report's point stronger. Street PSNR is Horizon-GS 23.66/20.62/20.34 vs Hierarchical-GS 23.59/21.13/20.47, so a ground-capable baseline matches or beats Horizon-GS at street level on 2 of 3 large scenes. Aerial is where Horizon-GS wins (28.89/31.09/29.34 vs Scaffold 27.62/25.46/23.91).

verdicts.claim: Horizon-GS ablation: removing camera balancing costs 0.74 dB, densification balancing 0.21 dB, multi-LOD 0.18 dB.
verdicts.correction: These are AERIAL PSNR deltas, measured on the real Road and Park scenes (Table 4). The matching STREET deltas are only -0.04, -0.06 and -0.01 dB. So the Horizon-GS mechanisms the report recommends reimplementing in gsplat (2:1 then 1:1 sampling, stage-wise densification, LOD) barely affect ground-level views. Porting them for option (b) would therefore buy almost nothing for a ground-walk viewer, which strengthens the case against (b). Schedule confirmed: stage 1 is 60k iterations at 2:1 aerial sampling with densification ending at 30k; stage 2 is 40k iterations at 1:1 with densification ending at 20k.

verdicts.claim: Horizon-GS real data used a DJI M350RTK with a 5-camera payload, a 6-camera helmet, transitional views and ContextCapture poses; images resized to 1600 px; A100 80 GB; about 4 h per large scene.
verdicts.correction: Further detail: the aerial cameras are 5 x 9552x6368 full-frame (36 mm); the helmet carries 6 x DJI Action4 at 3840x2160; transitional imagery was added for overlap; poses came from ContextCapture; the dataset has 5 synthetic and 2 real scenes.

verdicts.claim: Horizon-GS code is released under the Inria 3DGS non-commercial license, with a gsplat-based renderer.
verdicts.correction: The README says 'Please follow the LICENSE of 3D-GS' and that it uses a modified gsplat to unify the rendering of different Gaussian types. It has a Windows-only setup line (SET DISTUTILS_USE_SDK=1). The repo has only 5 commits, so expect little maintenance. Under the Inria license, commercial use needs explicit consent (stip-sophia.transfert@inria.fr).

verdicts.claim: UC-GS (BMVC 2024): uncertainty-weighted aerial pixels give road views +0.68 dB (NYC) and +0.41 dB (SF) on synthetic AirSim/UE data; naive A+G 'does not demonstrate remarkable improvements'; mainly helps shifted or tilted views.
verdicts.correction: Table 1 road-view PSNR. NYC: Scaffold ground-only 25.64, naive A+G 25.66, UC-GS 26.32. SF: 25.16, 24.98 (naive A+G is WORSE), 25.57. On shifted or tilted test views (+0.1 m, 5 deg down) the gain is about +0.9 / +0.8 dB. The report's open item is now resolved: the repo LICENSE.md is the Inria Gaussian-Splatting license, i.e. non-commercial.

verdicts.claim: DRAGON: COLMAP registered only 50.00% of mixed drone+ground views; synthetic intermediate-elevation renders raised this to 97.47%.
verdicts.correction: The numbers are right, but the data is semi-synthetic, not real capture: the Buildings-NVS set was rendered in Google Earth Studio, with 9 building scenes and 122 training images per building (61 drone, 61 ground). 50% is consistent with COLMAP registering only one of the two halves (inference). DRAGON reports 0.01 m and 0.12 deg average errors. The paper is a July 2024 arXiv preprint (Rice University). It is weaker evidence for real forests than the report implies.

verdicts.claim: AerialMegaDepth (CVPR 2025): off-the-shelf DUSt3R RRA@5 on aerial-ground pairs is 5.20%, and 55.96% after fine-tuning.
verdicts.correction: Also: MASt3R goes from 3.36% to 49.54%. The aerial training views are pseudo-synthetic renders from Google Earth meshes paired with MegaDepth ground photos (urban landmarks). The code and weights license is not stated on the project page or the repo excerpt (last update 5 Sep 2025); assume it inherits DUSt3R/MASt3R CC BY-NC-SA.

verdicts.claim: Sky2Ground (CVPR 2026, 51 sites): SkyNet gives +9.6% RRA@5 and +18.1% RTA@5 over MASt3R/VGGT-class methods; satellite views often degrade results.
verdicts.correction: The abstract states these as absolute improvements and lists MASt3R, DUSt3R, MapAnything and VGGT as benchmarked baselines. The dataset mixes synthetic and real images.

verdicts.claim: An Aug-2026 detector-free aerial-ground SfM reports +93.9% AUC@5 vs LoFTR.
verdicts.correction: The abstract says it 'improves AUC at 5 deg pose error by 93.9% compared with LoFTR'. This reads as a relative improvement, not +93.9 percentage points. ISfM precision improves 27.6-32.7%. The paper is urban-oriented, a rotation-robust detector-free matcher plus track refinement, and is not a forest study.

verdicts.claim: Local features (SIFT) degrade beyond ~25-30 deg out-of-plane viewpoint change; Lowe 2004 reports >50% matching accuracy up to ~50 deg on planar scenes.
verdicts.correction: The PMC6359040 review does state local intensity-patch features are 'robust up to 25 deg-30 deg' of viewpoint change. I could not check the Lowe 50 deg / 50% figure: the fetched PDF was not machine-readable and the review does not cite it. It is consistent with background knowledge (medium confidence). The conclusion stands: about 90 deg nadir-to-horizontal is far outside SIFT's range.

verdicts.claim: XGRIDS LCC Aerial-Ground Map Fusion needs RTK on both the drone (DJI M4E) and the scanner; the heliguy case used 30 m ortho + 70 m Smart Oblique cross-hatch, manual corner shots every 1 m up to 70 m, and ~5 h processing on an RTX 5090 with 128 GB RAM.
verdicts.correction: The scanner was an XGRIDS Lixel K1 and the article is dated 11 Jul 2025. Quote: 'the K1 and M4E required an RTK fix'. Take-off and landing imagery was also used for alignment. The quality claims are qualitative only (roof-tops, blind spots); no metrics are given. Missed in the report: heliguy/XGRIDS recommend a 16-core CPU, an RTX 3090 or better (ideally a 4090) and at least 64 GB RAM for fusion processing. That is above the user's RTX 3080 Ti laptop, and RAM is unknown.

verdicts.claim: DJI-Terra-oriented guides recommend compositing a georeferenced aerial splat with ground splats in SuperSplat/SplatForge; nadir 80-85% front / 70-80% side overlap; obliques needed.
verdicts.correction: thefuture3d (3 Apr 2026): '80%+ front, 70%+ side', with 85%/80% for the highest quality. It says nadir-only gives poor vertical surfaces and recommends Smart 3D Capture's five-direction obliques. It names DJI Terra V5.0+ as having native GS. Quote: 'georeferenced aerial GS provides the spatial framework; ground-level GS fills in detail'. Compositing separate layers (option c) is the mainstream practitioner workflow. I could not open the Pix4D community post (redirect loop), so the Pix4D-specific claims (informed transition, 85% oblique overlap, GCPs/MTPs) are unverified.

verdicts.claim: Swinfield et al. 2019: in dense tropical forest, gaps reaching the floor are rare or absent, so UAV-SfM usually cannot map the ground.
verdicts.correction: Remote Sensing 11(8):928. The abstract says 'it is often impossible to map the ground elevation directly from such data because canopy gaps are rare in rainforests'. It also reports that SfM underestimated canopy height by about 5 m against LiDAR in Indonesia. The MDPI full text returned 403, so the exact phrase 'very rare or absent' was not re-verified.

verdicts.claim: Brown et al. 2024 (boreal): DEM RMSE <1.5 m in all cases, 0.31 m over open terrain; overcast best for sparse-forest CHM, clear sky best for the forest class.
verdicts.correction: Full text was blocked (403), so the RMSE numbers are unverified. The abstract (Applied Vegetation Science 2024; Brown, Ghaly, Greiser, Lam, Lehmann; heterogeneous boreal landscape) confirms 'summer under overcast conditions' as best for sparse forest and 'summer under clear skies' as best for denser vegetation (CHM). The report left out that autumn with clear skies was most suitable for ELEVATION models across all vegetation types. So 'prefer overcast' is right for splat appearance consistency, but if the drone is meant for terrain it should fly at a different time. Points correlate with reference data up to R2 = 0.995.

verdicts.claim: Aerial-to-ground forest registration reaches decimetre accuracy: 0.24 m average canopy-shape TLS-ULS; 0.17 m tropical / 0.05 m northern ULS-MLS.
verdicts.correction: Forests 2025 (Yu et al.): DSM+FPFH coarse alignment then ICP, 6 plots, 0.24 m average in 5.14 s. Remote Sensing 2025 (Liang et al.): 0.17 m over 8 Malaysian tropical plots (canopy density 0.93) and 0.05 m over 6 northern-China plots (0.75). Both are LiDAR-to-LiDAR results, as the report says, so photogrammetric-to-BLK2GO registration should be expected to do worse. Casseau et al. 2024 (arXiv 2410.09896) is a markerless deformable pose-graph method; its accuracy figure is not in the abstract.

verdicts.claim: gsplat simple_trainer has antialiased (default False), app_opt/app_embed_dim=16, post_processing in {bilateral_grid, ppisp}, pose_opt (lr 1e-5), packed, sparse_grad, depth_loss; PPISP(num_cameras=parser.num_cameras, num_frames=len(trainset)); no per-image sampling weights.
verdicts.correction: The DataLoader uses shuffle=True with no sampler or weights, so camera-group balancing needs a custom WeightedRandomSampler or similar. Antialiased mode applies only the Mip-Splatting 2D opacity compensation rho=sqrt(det(Sigma)/det(Sigma+eps I)); the 3D smoothing filter is not mentioned in the docs. The latest tagged gsplat release seen is v1.5.3 (4 Jul 2025), so PPISP appears to be main-branch only. Pin a commit.

verdicts.claim: gsplat memory on Mip-NeRF360 (A100): MCMC 1M = 1.98 GB, MCMC 3M = 4.99 GB, default = 5.62 GB.
verdicts.correction: PSNR: 29.18, 29.65 and 29.00 respectively. Antialiased mode uses 5.87 GB (29.03) and absgrad 4.40 GB (29.11).

verdicts.claim: PPISP (NVIDIA, arXiv 2601.18336) is Apache-2.0 and gives per-camera and per-frame ISP compensation.
verdicts.correction: The nv-tlabs/ppisp repo is Apache-2.0. Per-camera parts: vignetting and CRF. Per-frame parts: exposure and colour correction (chromaticity homography). A controller predicts per-frame corrections for novel views. The arXiv entry was submitted 26 Jan 2026 and revised 7 Apr 2026. One fetch of the arXiv page reported 'CC BY 4.0'; that is most likely the paper's licence, not the code's.

verdicts.claim: Octree-GS (TPAMI 2025) is under the Inria NC license, supports MatrixCity and appearance embeddings, and uses 2.36 GB vs 3.70 GB on MatrixCity.
verdicts.correction: LICENSE.md is the Inria/MPII gaussian-splatting license. It was tested only on Ubuntu 18.04 with CUDA 11.6; prebuilt Windows viewers are provided, but Windows training is unverified.

verdicts.claim: CityGaussian is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; CityGS-X (ICCV 2025) README shows no license.
verdicts.correction: CityGaussian V2 (ICLR 2025) states CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. CityGS-X has no license stated, which by default grants NO reuse rights at all, worse than NC. It supports single-GPU training and was tested on Ubuntu 18.04 / CUDA 11.6.

verdicts.claim: LichtFeld Studio is GPLv3, with MCMC, bilateral grid and 3DGUT; needs CUDA 12.8+ and driver 570+.
verdicts.correction: It also needs compute capability 7.5+ and C++23. New nuance: prebuilt Windows binaries are distributed through the paid LichtFeld Portal; source builds remain free under GPLv3. GPLv3 is copyleft, which matters if it is embedded in a distributed Hexagon tool.

verdicts.claim: MASt3R is CC BY-NC-SA; RoMa is MIT; LightGlue is Apache-2.0.
verdicts.correction: A licensing trap is missing from the report. The LightGlue README says SuperPoint (weights and inference file) is under a separate restrictive Magic Leap license. For a commercial path use ALIKED (BSD-3) or DISK (Apache-2.0) with LightGlue, never SuperPoint.

verdicts.claim: COLMAP: 3.11 pose-prior mapper; 4.0 global mapper + ALIKED/LightGlue; 4.2 multi-component reconstruction (release dates looked inconsistent).
verdicts.correction: The features are confirmed on the release tag pages. 3.11.0 (28 Nov 2024): 'pose prior based incremental mapper that can leverage absolute pose priors from e.g. GPS'. 4.0.0: GLOMAP as global_mapper, ALIKED N16Rot/N32 and LightGlue via ONNX, pose priors tied to sensor data, rigs. 4.1.0: spherical (equirectangular) camera models, the Caspar GPU BA backend and EXIF gravity priors. 4.2.0: multi-component global mapper ('disconnected view-graph components are reconstructed independently and returned as separate models') and LoMa learned features. Release dates are still inconsistent between the list page and the tag pages; the tag pages say 4.0 Mar 2025, 4.1 Jun 2025, 4.2 Sep 2025. Treat the dates as unverified.

verdicts.claim: A C0 Mini-class drone (DJI Mini 4 Pro: 1/1.3-inch, 8064x6048, 82.1 deg) at 30 m gives about 5.2 mm/px at 48 MP; Insta360 8K equirect gives about 1.6 mm/px at 2 m and about 12 mm/px at 15 m.
verdicts.correction: DJI specs confirm C0 (EU), <249 g, 48 MP, 8064x6048, 82.1 deg FOV, GPS+Galileo+BeiDou, 34 min. The arithmetic checks out: 30 m x 2 x tan(41.05 deg) x 0.8 = 41.8 m, / 8064 = 5.18 mm/px; 2*pi/7680 = 0.818 mrad. The Mini 4 Pro is no longer the best C0 choice; the Mini 5 Pro is better (see missed developments). The spec fetch also claimed a mechanical shutter on the Mini 4 Pro. That is doubtful (background knowledge says electronic only), so keep the report's hover-and-shoot advice.

verdicts.claim: Antigravity A1 (Insta360-incubated): 249 g, 8K 360, 1/1.28-inch 55 MP, 24/39 min, announced Aug 2025, available Dec 2025.
verdicts.correction: With the high-capacity battery it weighs 291 g, so it would leave the sub-250 g C0 regime. Its EU class mark is still unverified.

verdicts.claim: 'LiDAR-Guided Semantic 3DGS for Forest Digital Twins' (Remote Sensing 2026) fuses handheld LiDAR with UAV images: PSNR 24.94, SSIM 0.773, LPIPS 0.231, DBH R2 0.848, RMSE 2.705 cm.
verdicts.correction: The abstract confirms all the numbers across three plots and says the method beats NeRF and baseline 3DGS. It is explicitly scoped to 'open-canopy forest environments such as urban and campus forests', and the abstract mentions no ground-level imagery. It supports the idea that LiDAR anchors help UAV-image splats in open canopy, and says nothing about closed or tropical canopy.

verdicts.claim: Foliage motion from wind and rotor downwash breaks the static-scene assumption (realhorizons source).
verdicts.correction: The Real Horizons guide (Jun 2026, updated Jul 2026) advises against making 'a moving tree canopy the main visual anchor for camera recovery' and recommends keeping the sun on the same side of surfaces. It does NOT discuss rotor downwash. The downwash part is the researcher's own inference and should be labelled that way.

missed_developments.claim: Spark 2.x (Three.js splat renderer) sorts multiple SplatMesh objects together in one depth sort, with LoD and a splat budget. This answers the report's open question on depth-sorting two layers.
missed_developments.details: Spark 2.3.1 docs: 'Multi-Splat Tree Traversal' supports multiple independently positioned splat trees in a single sort, so splats from different files interleave correctly. LoD is a hierarchical splat tree cut under a fixed budget: 1.5M splats by default on desktop, 500K on mobile. LoD trees can be built on demand in a WebWorker or prebuilt, about 30% larger than the SPZ. For option (c) this means the aerial and ground splats can be shown together and cross-faded without a hard switch. The two layers must still be volume-partitioned (e.g. by the LiDAR CHM, as the report proposes) to avoid double surfaces. Both layers also share one mobile budget of about 500K.

missed_developments.claim: In Sweden, publishing or sharing aerial imagery requires a dissemination permit (spridningstillstånd) from Lantmäteriet. This affects any web-delivered drone layer, for (b) and (c) alike.
missed_developments.details: Lantmäteriet: 'Om du vill publicera, sälja eller dela material som avbildar Sverige från luften behöver du ansöka om spridningstillstånd från oss.' Material depicting sea may instead need a permit from Sjöfartsverket. The page does not say whether 3D models or splats derived from drone images count; the conservative assumption is yes (inference). Plan permit lead time before putting a drone-derived layer in a public or shared browser viewer. Internal-only R&D viewing is less clear. Ask Lantmäteriet.

missed_developments.claim: Swedish operator rules: any camera drone, even C0 under 250 g, needs Transportstyrelsen operator registration. Flying without a drone certificate (250 g+) has been punishable since 1 Jan 2026.
missed_developments.details: Registration is required for UAS of 250 g+, or with a camera or sensor able to capture personal data, or above 80 J, or in the specific category. The fee is SEK 190 plus SEK 250 per year. A1/A3 online theory test for 250 g+. Open category: max 120 m AGL, VLOS, A3 keeps 150 m horizontally from residential, industrial and recreational areas and 30 m from uninvolved people. Tighter penalties from 1 Jan 2026; SORA 2.5 methodology published 30 Sep 2025 for specific-category operations. Flying 20-30 m above a 20-25 m canopy is about 45-55 m AGL, within 120 m. Background knowledge, low confidence: nature reserves and national parks may have local drone bans; check the reserve regulations.

missed_developments.claim: The DJI Mini 5 Pro (2025) is a better current C0 candidate than the Mini 4 Pro the report used.
missed_developments.details: 1-inch CMOS, 50 MP (8192x6144), 84 deg FOV, 24 mm equivalent, electronic shutter, 249.9 g +/- 4 g, GPS+Galileo+BeiDou, 36 min (52 min with Battery Plus). It is C0-certified in the Fly More Combo, but C1 with the Combo Plus (Battery Plus), and C1 brings A1/A3 competency requirements. The electronic shutter keeps the hover-and-shoot advice valid. At 30 m it gives roughly 5 mm/px (calculation).

missed_developments.claim: Feed-forward pose models now have commercially usable variants, which the report did not list as permissive matcher or pose options.
missed_developments.details: VGGT-1B-Commercial (released 29 Jul 2025, gated application, military use excluded) is licensed for commercial use; the original VGGT-1B is non-commercial. MapAnything has an Apache-2.0 code and weights variant (facebook/map-anything-apache) alongside a CC-BY-NC one, and accepts intrinsics, poses and metric depth as inputs (3DV 2026). Caveat: Sky2Ground shows these models fail under large altitude gaps, so they do not change the conclusion that aerial-ground matching in a forest is unreliable.

missed_developments.claim: The commercial aerial-ground fusion vendor recommends hardware above the user's laptop.
missed_developments.details: heliguy/XGRIDS recommend a 16-core CPU (Ryzen 9 9950X class), an RTX 3090 or better (ideally a 4090) and at least 64 GB RAM for aerial-ground fusion. Their case study ran 5 h on an RTX 5090 with 128 GB RAM. The RTX 3080 Ti laptop (16 GB) is below this, which supports keeping (b) out of scope on this hardware.

missed_developments.claim: COLMAP 4.1 added native spherical (equirectangular) camera models and 4.2 added LoMa learned features plus the multi-component global mapper.
missed_developments.details: Native equirect support affects the bridging-capture idea of an Insta360 on a 3-5 m pole: 360 frames could enter a joint SfM without cubemap splitting. The multi-component global mapper returns drone and ground images as separate models when they do not connect, which is the expected outcome in a forest; it fits option (c), where each component is registered to the LiDAR separately.

missed_developments.claim: The evidence base is even more synthetic than the report says.
missed_developments.details: MatrixCity (UE synthetic), UC-GS (AirSim/UE synthetic), DRAGON (Google Earth Studio semi-synthetic) and AerialMegaDepth (pseudo-synthetic Google Earth aerial) are all synthetic or semi-synthetic. Horizon-GS has only 2 real urban scenes. The only real forest UAV+LiDAR GS paper (Remote Sensing 2026) covers open-canopy urban and campus forest. I could not search further for real aerial+ground forest splat studies because the shared WebSearch budget was used up before this check started; that gap remains open.

verification.recommendation_assessment:
The recommendations hold up. Independent checks support (a) for Phase 1, (c) as the later optional drone phase, and (b) as research-only, and none of the evidence argues for bringing the drone forward. Every paper number I could re-check matched: Horizon-GS Tables 1 and 2, UC-GS, AerialMegaDepth, Sky2Ground, the 2608.15251 paper, the gsplat memory figures, and the registration RMSEs. Several corrections make the case against (b) stronger:
(1) The Horizon-GS ablations the report wants to port (camera balancing, densification balancing, LOD) change STREET PSNR by only -0.04, -0.06 and -0.01 dB. All their benefit is in aerial views. On large scenes, Hierarchical-GS matches or beats Horizon-GS at street level on 2 of 3 scenes.
(2) The naive A+G result in UC-GS is +0.02 dB (NYC) and -0.18 dB (SF).
(3) The DRAGON, MatrixCity, UC-GS and AerialMegaDepth evidence is synthetic or semi-synthetic.
(4) The commercial fusion vendor recommends at least an RTX 3090/4090 and 64 GB RAM, above the user's laptop.

Changes I would make:
(a) Add a regulatory gate to the drone phase. In Sweden, publishing or sharing aerial imagery needs a Lantmäteriet dissemination permit, which very likely covers a drone-derived layer in a web viewer. Transportstyrelsen operator registration is needed even for a C0 camera drone (SEK 190 plus SEK 250 per year). Flying without the required certificate has been punishable since 1 Jan 2026.
(b) Recommend the DJI Mini 5 Pro (1-inch, 50 MP, C0 with the standard battery only) over the Mini 4 Pro as the default C0 class.
(c) Resolve the viewer open question: Spark 2.x sorts multiple splat layers together with LoD (1.5M desktop / 500K mobile budget), so (c) can cross-fade layers without a hard switch. Keep the CHM-based volume partition to avoid double surfaces, and budget the shared mobile splat count.
(d) In the (b) technique, pair LightGlue only with ALIKED (BSD-3) or DISK (Apache), never SuperPoint (restrictive license). Add VGGT-1B-Commercial and MapAnything-apache as permissive learned-pose options, while noting they fail under large altitude gaps.
(e) Downgrade the plan to 'reimplement Horizon-GS sampling and densification in gsplat' for (b). Its measured benefit is aerial-only, so a loose merge with pose_opt is enough as the research experiment.
(f) Make the capture-timing advice more precise. Brown 2024 found overcast best only for sparse-forest CHM in summer, clear sky best for denser forest, and autumn clear sky best for DEMs. Overcast is still right for splat appearance consistency.
(g) Treat the claims on rotor downwash and Lowe's 50 deg figure as inference or background knowledge.
(h) Treat the UC-GS and CityGS-X code as unusable for a commercial path: UC-GS is confirmed Inria non-commercial, and CityGS-X has no license at all.

Caveat: the shared web-search budget ran out before this check started, so I could not search for new real-data aerial+ground forest splat studies. All verification above used direct fetches of primary pages.

research.summary:
BOTTOM LINE: A drone camera above a forest records the canopy top, crown shapes, gaps, terrain in open areas and the surroundings. It records very little of the forest floor or understory, and almost none in tropical rainforest. Aerial and under-canopy ground views share almost no surfaces, so putting them into one SfM/splat (option b) is the riskiest and least useful choice for this project. Recommendation: keep the first test as (a) LiDAR + Insta360. Add the drone later as an optional, separately reconstructed AERIAL LAYER (option c). Register it to the LiDAR frame and show it in the same viewer with fading based on camera height and region. Do not merge it into the ground splat.

VISIBILITY THROUGH CANOPY. Forestry remote-sensing work agrees: UAV photogrammetry (SfM/DAP) rebuilds only the visible top-of-canopy surface. It gets ground points only where gaps are big enough to be lit and seen from the oblique angles that triangulation needs. Wallace et al. 2016 (eucalypt): as canopy got denser, SfM gave <1 ground point/m² while UAV LiDAR still mapped the terrain. Jayathunga et al. 2018: where non-ground cover was >0.95, DAP-only estimates broke down (R²=0.20). With a LiDAR DTM they reached R²=0.91. In tropical rainforest, Swinfield et al. 2019 (Borneo) say it is 'often impossible' to map the ground from SfM because gaps are rare. Roşca et al. 2018 (Guyana) found that UAV SfM overstated heights inside gaps and missed small gaps altogether. Rainforest canopies block about 96% of laser shots and leave a few % of light at the floor (Amazon example: 673 ground returns out of more than 600k). Swedish boreal/hemiboreal stands are much more open, but they vary by species. Measured canopy transmittance is 0.12–0.89 in Scots pine and 0.04–0.40 in spruce (British data used as a proxy). The Swedish national programme estimates forest variables from aerial image matching plus a separate ALS DEM, because image matching gives the canopy surface but not the terrain. Expected result: in a thinned pine or birch stand, oblique drone images will show some trunks and ground patches. TreeDGS measured DBH from 70/90 m oblique Matrice 4E images in a pine plantation, but the breast-height band was often hidden and fully hidden stems could not be recovered. In spruce, and in any tropical forest, the drone gives canopy, terrain and context only. Drone LiDAR gets through much better (understory DEM RMSE ≤0.24 m where cover is <0.9), but it is a different sensor class.

WHAT DRONE IMAGERY IS GOOD FOR: top-of-canopy height and crown shapes, gaps, forest edges, terrain and context around the plot, and an overview mode in the viewer. It also fills a real hole in ground-only capture. Handheld and terrestrial scanning hides the upper crowns and underestimates tree height (one HMLS study: bias −2.34 m). Aerial and terrestrial clouds together cover a wider range of tree heights (Casseau/Fallon IROS 2024). This matters most in tropical forests, where a BLK2GO and an Insta360 at 1.5 m height will never see the top of a canopy 30–50 m up.

MERGED SPLAT PROBLEMS (evidence comes mostly from urban scenes, which are easier than forests). COLMAP-class SfM fails between aerial and ground images. DRAGON: plain COLMAP registered only about 50% of a drone+ground set, and it worked only after 'bridge' images at intermediate heights were added. AerialMegaDepth: DUSt3R placed fewer than 5% of aerial-ground pairs within 5°. SIFT often finds zero correct matches. Horizon-GS (CVPR 2025) reports that joint training causes conflicting densification: street views prune Gaussians that aerial views regrow. The jointly trained model scored below both separately trained ones. It also needed ContextCapture poses, extra transitional views and A100-80GB GPUs, and it uses the non-commercial Inria license. The commercial XGRIDS aerial-ground fusion requires an RTK fix on both devices plus 'vertical photo towers' (ascent sequences) as bridges. A BLK2GO has no GNSS, RTK under canopy is unreliable, and bridging ascents are only possible in clearings or at forest edges. In a forest, the drone sees the tops of the crowns and the ground camera sees the trunks and the undersides of the crowns, so there are almost no shared features. One 2026 paper did fuse handheld SLAM LiDAR with UAV imagery in a 3DGS forest twin (PSNR 24.94), but it aligned through point-cloud registration and LiDAR anchors, not through joint image matching. Because the viewer limits navigation to the LiDAR ground, aerial Gaussians in a merged model would mostly be seen from below, through the lower canopy. Expected gain at walking height: small. Risk of floaters, double canopy and lost detail: real.

SEPARATE LAYER (option c). Train the aerial splat, or build a mesh/DSM/orthophoto, with standard single-domain tools. Register it to the LiDAR frame using GCP targets placed in gaps and scanned by the BLK2GO (cm level), drone RTK/PPK georeferencing, ICP of the drone canopy and gap-ground points against the upper LiDAR points, or tree-position matching (0.31–0.44 m RMSE in published work). Expect 0.1–0.5 m residuals. Avoid content overlap: crop the aerial layer to the canopy top and surroundings, crop the ground splat above the canopy, and fade between them by camera height above the LiDAR DTM. Current web renderers handle two splat objects correctly. Spark sorts all SplatMeshes in one global sort, Spark 2.0 (Apr 2026) runs joint LoD across several objects under one budget (500K–2.5M splats), and SplatMesh has a global opacity. PlayCanvas unified rendering also sorts all GSplat components together. GaussianSplats3D is unmaintained. Separate training also keeps peak VRAM within 16 GB.

UNDER-CANOPY DRONE. Research systems work but are fragile. An autonomous Finnish prototype succeeded on 87.5% of missions in a difficult stand of 2,000 trees/ha, with emergency stops caused by thin dry branches, a trajectory error of 0.34–0.50 m and 1 m/s flight. Consumer options: DJI Avata 360 (Mar 2026, 455 g, 8K/60 360°, omnidirectional sensing, prop guards) and Antigravity A1 (249 g, 8K 360°, but only front and bottom sensing). For this project, handheld 360 capture alongside the BLK2GO is better: it follows the same path, is easier to time-sync and has no crash risk. To add camera heights of 2–5 m, a telescopic pole is a cheaper option (not researched; background knowledge). In tropical understory the low light, vines and need for VLOS (visual line of sight) make it worse still.

VERDICTS. Sweden: (a) for the first test. A drone gives little benefit for a 10×10 m plot. If context is wanted, try free Lantmäteriet open data first (ALS point cloud, 1–2 pts/m²; 1 m DTM; 0.16/0.4 m orthophotos) as a context layer, then (c) as an optional phase. Tropical: (c) is clearly worth it for canopy-top documentation, but never for the floor. (b) is not recommended in either case, except as research at a forest edge or clearing with bridging captures.

findings.claim: UAV RGB photogrammetry reconstructs mainly the top-of-canopy surface. It gets ground/terrain only where canopy gaps are large enough, and fails under near-closed canopy.
findings.details: Wallace et al. 2016 (30x50 m eucalypt plot, mixed cover): SfM underperformed UAV LiDAR on terrain as canopy got denser, with <1 ground point/m² and a 0.12 m mean difference from the ALS terrain. Jayathunga et al. 2018: where non-ground coverage was >0.95, DAP-only estimates were poor (R²=0.20, RMSE 12.34 m); using a LiDAR DTM gave R²=0.91, RMSE 1.61 m. Iglhaut et al. 2019 review: SfM is accurate on visible crowns, but its main limitation is the ground surface, which is defined only where large gaps exist. Tomaštík 2017: photogrammetric terrain was usable (<20 cm vertical) only under partially open canopy.

findings.claim: In tropical rainforest, a drone camera sees essentially none of the forest floor. SfM ground mapping is 'often impossible' because gaps are rare, and SfM even misrepresents the gaps that do exist.
findings.details: Swinfield et al. 2019 (Maliau Basin, Sabah): SfM rarely reaches the ground because canopy openings are too small to be lit the same as the canopy, or to be seen from the oblique angles needed for triangulation; they used a LiDAR DTM. Roşca et al. 2018 (Guyana, 650 trees/ha): UAV SfM top-of-canopy models matched TLS within 0.5 m in 71–77% of pixels but overestimated height inside gaps (99th percentile +11.42 m), often missed small gaps, and showed positive height bias over >85% of the area in 7 of 14 gaps. Reported Amazon values: about 96% canopy cover, about 4% gap fraction, about 5.7% of PAR reaching 1 m above the floor; thick rainforest blocks up to 96% of laser shots (vs 70–80% in temperate forest), and one Amazon example had only 673 ground returns out of more than 600k.

findings.claim: Swedish and boreal forests are far more open than rainforest, but floor visibility from above depends strongly on species and stand. Thinned pine and leaf-off birch show patches of floor and some trunks; spruce shows little.
findings.details: Canopy transmittance in British studies (proxy for vertical gap fraction): Scots pine 0.12–0.89, Sitka spruce 0.04–0.40. Norway spruce LAI 3.1–8.2 is typical. Swedish forest land is defined by crown cover >10%, so stands vary widely. The SLU method for hemiboreal southern Sweden (Bohlin et al. 2012) combines aerial image matching (canopy surface) with a separate high-resolution ALS DEM, because image matching gives the canopy, not the terrain. The view-angle effect is background physics: gap probability falls roughly as exp(-k·LAI/cosθ), so oblique views see the floor less often per ray but see trunk sides more. TreeDGS (Matrice 4E, 70 m and 90 m incl. oblique, GSD about 1.84 cm, 365 images/plot, loblolly pine plantation) measured DBH from the air (RMSE 4.79 cm), but the breast-height band was 'frequently occluded by crowns, branches, and understory', and fully occluded stems could not be recovered.

findings.claim: Drone LiDAR (ULS) gets through canopy far better than drone photogrammetry, but it is a different sensor and cost class.
findings.details: For canopy cover <0.9, understory DEMs from UAV LiDAR had MAE ≤0.17 m and RMSE ≤0.24 m (J. Mountain Science 2024). UAV LiDAR beat UAV DAP on forest attributes (R² 0.58–0.91 vs 0.52–0.83). DJI Zenmuse L2: 5 returns and a 4x12 cm spot at 100 m. A drone photo set cannot replace this, and the project's ground terrain already comes from the BLK2GO.

findings.claim: The real value of the drone is that it fills what ground capture cannot see: upper crowns and canopy top, gaps, forest edges and surroundings. Ground-based scanning hides the upper canopy and underestimates tree height.
findings.details: MLS/TLS work from the ground, so upper parts of trees are hidden; ULS gives tree height better, while MLS gives DBH and stems better (Ghent comparison). One HMLS study reported tree-height RMSE of 2.85 m with a −2.34 m bias. Casseau/Fallon (IROS 2024, Evo Finland + Switzerland): combined aerial and terrestrial clouds 'cover a larger range of tree heights'. A combined backpack/handheld plus above-canopy ULS approach gave about 10% stem-volume RMSE. In tropical forests, with canopies around 30–50 m, the BLK2GO and Insta360 at 1.5 m will not see the canopy top.

findings.claim: Joint SfM registration of aerial and ground images commonly fails, even in textured urban scenes. It works only with bridging intermediate-altitude images, special matchers or RTK on all devices.
findings.details: DRAGON: plain COLMAP registered only about 50% of a drone+ground set; registration succeeds 'when intermediate level images are provided, serving as a bridge' (97.47% with the method). AerialMegaDepth (CVPR 2025): DUSt3R placed fewer than 5% of aerial-ground pairs within 5° of rotation error, and about 56% after fine-tuning on a purpose-built dataset. 3DGS intermediate-view matching (2025): SIFT and SuperGlue gave 0 correct matches on several aerial-ground pairs. Sky2Ground (2026): sparse geometric overlap and large altitude ranges degrade current SOTA methods (MASt3R, VGGT). Inference, not yet published for forests: shared surfaces between canopy-top and under-canopy views are close to zero, so a forest is harder than these urban cases.

findings.claim: Training one 3DGS model on aerial and ground views together harms quality unless specialised methods are used. Those methods need heavy hardware and come with restrictive licenses.
findings.details: Horizon-GS (CVPR 2025): 'While street views cause the densification policy to remove irrelevant, occluded Gaussians, aerial views promote regrowth in these regions'. Joint training underperformed both aerial-only and street-only training. Real scenes needed ContextCapture poses plus 'transitional views'. Training ran on A100 80 GB, about 4 h per large scene. The code follows the Inria 3DGS license (non-commercial). CrossView-GS likewise reconstructs aerial and ground in separate branches before merging. These methods support training the sources separately and combining them afterwards.

findings.claim: Commercial aerial-ground splat fusion (XGRIDS Lixel CyberColor) requires an RTK fix on both the handheld scanner and the drone, plus vertical 'photo tower' ascent sequences. The BLK2GO workflow cannot meet the first condition, and the second is possible only in clearings or at forest edges.
findings.details: E38/Heliguy workflow: both devices must hold an active RTK fix or fusion fails. The drone flies grid/nadir passes plus 3–4 vertical image series, taking frames at 1 s intervals while climbing from ground to mapping altitude, and takeoff/landing images 'tie the ground scan to the aerial photos'. The only case study shown is a building. Processing took about 5 h on an RTX 5090 with 128 GB RAM. The BLK2GO has no GNSS, and RTK under canopy ranges from cm-level to metres (review of 25 studies).

findings.claim: The closest published forest analogue fused handheld SLAM LiDAR with UAV imagery in one 3DGS model. Alignment came from point-cloud registration and LiDAR anchors, not joint image matching, and the absolute image quality was modest.
findings.details: Remote Sensing 18(11):1696 (2026): coarse-to-fine registration of the UAV SfM point cloud to handheld LiDAR; LiDAR geometric anchors to initialise 3DGS; wood/leaf semantic constraints. Results: PSNR 24.94 dB, SSIM 0.773, LPIPS 0.231; DBH R²=0.848, RMSE 2.705 cm. The full text was blocked (403), so UAV altitude (above or below canopy) and the per-view breakdown are unverified. This is a counterpoint: merging is possible when LiDAR is the backbone. It is not evidence that a merged model looks better than separate layers at walking height.

findings.claim: Markerless registration of aerial data to ground LiDAR in forests works through tree positions or canopy shape, but only to decimetre level. Dense canopy makes treetop detection harder.
findings.details: Casseau/Fallon (IROS 2024): aerial (ULS) treetops from the CHM matched to ground (backpack Hesai XT32) stem positions via a deformable pose graph. Point-to-point RMSE 0.44 m (Evo, Finland, boreal pine/spruce) and 0.31 m (Stein am Rhein, Switzerland, mixed). Authors: 'for dense forest environments it is likely to be more difficult to distinguish individual treetops due to canopy overlap'. Above- and under-canopy ULS registered with targets in Leica Cyclone gave 0.4 cm mean error. So targets visible from both views give cm-level results; natural features give about 0.3–0.5 m.

findings.claim: Web splat renderers that fit this stack handle two or more separate splat objects with one correct global sort and a shared LoD budget. A separate aerial layer is therefore technically easy to render. Artifacts come from overlapping content, not from sorting.
findings.details: Spark: SplatMeshes are collected by a SplatAccumulator and bucket-sorted together, 'merging with other opaque THREE.js geometry using the Z buffer'. Spark 2.0 (released around 2026-04-15) does 'LoD rendering across multiple splat objects simultaneously, traversing multiple trees jointly', with a global budget of 500K–2.5M splats by device and the streamable .RAD format. SplatMesh.opacity is a global opacity multiplier usable for height-based fading, and SplatEdits/SDF can crop. PlayCanvas unified rendering: 'All splats from all GSplat components are sorted together in a single global sort'; its budget guidance is about 1M splats on mobile and 3M+ on desktop. mkkellogg GaussianSplats3D is no longer actively developed and points users to Spark.

findings.claim: Under-canopy drone flight works in research but is fragile. For this project it does not beat handheld 360 capture alongside the BLK2GO.
findings.details: Finnish autonomous under-canopy prototype (2025): 1.15 kg, RealSense D435 plus Jetson Orin NX, 1 m/s, 2.25–2.75 m altitude, 34–42 m flights. 100% mission success in a medium stand (650 trees/ha) and 87.5% in a difficult stand (2,000 trees/ha, spruce), where thin dry spruce branches went undetected and forced emergency stops. ATE 0.34–0.50 m; DBH RMSE 3.33 cm; 79% stem completeness. Under-canopy ULS (Hyyppä 2020) reached DBH RMSE 0.60 cm in sparse boreal stands with manual piloting. Krisanski 2020 used a DJI Phantom 4 below canopy (DBH RMSE 1.1–2.1 cm). Handheld 360 has the same trajectory as the LiDAR, easy time sync and no crash risk. Prop wash moving foliage and low understory light causing motion blur are background knowledge (low confidence).

findings.claim: Consumer 360 drones exist that could act as a 'flying Insta360' under or at the edge of canopy. The DJI Avata 360 suits this better than the Antigravity A1 because it senses obstacles in all directions and has prop guards.
findings.details: DJI Avata 360 (announced 2026-03-26, shipping Apr 2026): 455 g; two 1/1.1-inch sensors; 8K/60 HDR 360 video; 120 MP 360 photos; 180 Mbps; omnidirectional obstacle sensing in 360 mode plus forward LiDAR; integrated prop guards; about 23 min flight; USD 719 with RC 2. EU class label not verified (C1 expected for 250–900 g, unconfirmed). Antigravity A1 (Insta360 spin-off): 249 g (C0); two 1/1.28-inch sensors; 8K/30 360; obstacle sensing only front and down, and off in Sport mode; thin props without guards. The reviewer warns that dense forest flying needs manual avoidance and that effective resolution is closer to 2.7K–4K per direction. From USD 1,599.

findings.claim: For Swedish sites, free national open data can provide an aerial context layer without flying a drone.
findings.details: Lantmäteriet 'Laserdata Nedladdning, skog' is an open, classified ALS point cloud at 1–2 pts/m². 'Markhöjdmodell Nedladdning, grid 1+' is a 1 m DTM. Orthophotos became open data on 3 Feb 2025, at 0.16 m or 0.4 m, with about 30% of Sweden re-flown each year (2–10 year cycle), served via STAC (api.lantmateriet.se/stac-bild/v1/). The exact license (CC0) for each Lantmäteriet product was not confirmed on a primary page; Skogsstyrelsen data is CC0. Coarse, but enough for surroundings, terrain context and approximate georeferencing.

findings.claim: Forest canopy imagery is hard for SfM in any case. It needs very high overlap, and wind and lighting affect results.
findings.details: Frey et al. 2018: completeness kept improving with overlap, and was best at ≥95% forward overlap. Recent guidance: 90% forward / 85% side at 120 m. A minimum of 80% is widely recommended for irregular canopy. Uniform canopy texture, repeating patterns and tree movement cause noise. Dandois et al. 2015 studied altitude, overlap, wind, cloud and light. Lighting detail from background knowledge: diffuse or overcast light helps, so fly under the same overcast conditions as the ground capture.

recommendations.recommendation: Keep the first Swedish test as option (a), LiDAR + Insta360 only. Do not buy a drone or plan flights for phase 1.
recommendations.rationale: A 10x10 m plot gains little from above: the viewer limits navigation to the LiDAR ground, so aerial content would mostly be seen from below through the lower canopy. Merging is the riskiest path: joint SfM fails, densification conflicts, and the BLK2GO has no RTK. Phase 1 should prove registering the splat to the LiDAR first.
recommendations.alternatives: If the user wants context in phase 1, add a zero-cost 'aerial context' layer from Lantmäteriet open ALS, DTM and orthophoto instead of flying.

recommendations.recommendation: Make the drone a later, optional phase built as option (c): a separate aerial model (splat for photoreal views, plus optional DSM/orthophoto or mesh) registered into the LiDAR frame and shown as its own viewer layer. Do not choose (b), one merged splat.
recommendations.rationale: Published evidence points to separate reconstruction followed by combination. Horizon-GS shows joint training below both single-domain models, CrossView-GS uses separate branches, and DRAGON/AerialMegaDepth show joint registration failing. Forests have even less shared content between aerial and ground views. Separate training also fits 16 GB VRAM, uses standard open tools for each source, and matches the modular source architecture.
recommendations.alternatives: (b) only as a research experiment at a forest edge or clearing, with bridging 'photo tower' ascents and targets, and a LiDAR-anchored joint optimisation like the 2026 forest digital-twin paper. Expect a lot of engineering and possible quality loss.

recommendations.recommendation: Plug the drone module into the common source interface with these outputs: a reconstruction (splat .ply/.spz/.rad, optional DSM/ortho GeoTIFF or mesh), a 4x4 similarity transform into the shared frame with residuals, a coverage polygon, a valid height band (e.g. canopy top and above), and its georeference if any. Rules for the shared frame: LiDAR frame when LiDAR is present; otherwise the drone's georeferenced frame (GNSS/RTK EXIF gives metric scale and orientation); otherwise an arbitrary frame.
recommendations.rationale: The drone is the only source that can carry an absolute georeference (BLK2GO has no GNSS). Treating the georeference as optional metadata on the shared frame lets the 'drone only' and 'drone + splat' combinations work without LiDAR.
recommendations.alternatives: Always force a georeferenced ENU frame and attach the LiDAR to it. This adds a GCP or RTK dependency for every combination that includes LiDAR.

recommendations.recommendation: Register drone to LiDAR in order of preference: (1) 3–5 large targets (checkerboard, ≥0.5 m) placed in canopy gaps or at the plot edge, seen by the drone and scanned or photographed by the BLK2GO and Insta360 (cm level); (2) drone RTK/PPK georeferencing plus ICP of the drone dense cloud (gap ground and canopy) against the upper LiDAR points; (3) markerless matching of tree positions or canopy shape as a fallback (expect 0.3–0.5 m). Keep the user-measured device offset and a software check, as in the existing ground alignment.
recommendations.rationale: Natural-feature aerial-to-terrestrial registration in forests reaches only 0.31–0.44 m RMSE, which shows visibly if the layers overlap. Targets give cm-level results. Joint image matching is not viable under canopy.
recommendations.alternatives: Joint SfM with ground images, possible only where the plot touches a clearing and bridging ascent images are captured.

recommendations.recommendation: Viewer composition: split the content so the two layers do not overlap. Crop the aerial layer to the canopy top and the area outside the plot, and crop ground-splat floaters above the canopy. Fade the aerial layer in by camera height above the LiDAR DTM (e.g. hidden below canopy base, full above canopy top) using SplatMesh.opacity. Render both under one Spark 2.0 budget with joint LoD, or use PlayCanvas unified mode.
recommendations.rationale: Spark and PlayCanvas sort all splat objects together, so sorting is solved. The remaining artifacts are double canopy and ghosting from decimetre misregistration, and these are avoided by not overlapping the content. Shared budgets keep phones at about 0.5–1M splats.
recommendations.alternatives: Show the aerial model as a textured mesh or DSM plus orthophoto (lighter, robust on mobile, good for LuciadRIA) and keep splats only for the ground.

recommendations.recommendation: Do not use an under-canopy drone for understory capture. If extra camera heights are wanted for mid-canopy, use the Insta360 on a 3–5 m telescopic pole along the BLK2GO loop. Consider a 360 drone with omnidirectional sensing and guards (e.g. DJI Avata 360) only for forest-edge or clearing 'bridge' shots.
recommendations.rationale: Under-canopy drones work in research but are fragile: thin branches go undetected and there is no GNSS. Handheld capture keeps the same path and time sync as the LiDAR. Antigravity A1 lacks side, rear and up sensing.
recommendations.alternatives: Manually piloted cinewhoop (Avata 2) at walking pace for 2–6 m heights in open pine stands only, with a spotter.

recommendations.recommendation: Tropical phase: plan the drone as a canopy-top and context layer only (option c). Fly from a clearing, river or road where VLOS and takeoff are possible. Never expect it to add understory or floor content. If terrain under canopy is needed beyond the BLK2GO's reach, budget for drone LiDAR rather than photos.
recommendations.rationale: Rainforest canopy blocks about 96% of laser shots and SfM rarely reaches the ground. The ground devices cannot see a canopy top 30–50 m up, so in the tropics the drone adds the most information.
recommendations.alternatives: Skip the aerial layer and accept a ground-only model with a blurry or absent canopy top.

recommendations.recommendation: Capture protocol hints for a later drone phase (to be reconciled with the capture-strategy and regulations research): grid plus oblique passes (camera about 45–60° off nadir) and one or two orbits around the plot at 30–70 m AGL. Use ≥90% forward and ≥80–85% side overlap, still photos rather than video, and a fixed exposure set for the canopy. Fly within about 1 h of the ground capture, preferably under uniform overcast, with low wind. In Sweden, a leaf-off flight sees more floor in birch and aspen but will not match a leaf-on ground splat.
recommendations.rationale: Forest SfM completeness rises with overlap up to about 95%. Obliques improve gap and stem visibility (TreeDGS, Swinfield). Matching light reduces the appearance gap between layers.
recommendations.alternatives: Single nadir grid only, which gives a DSM and orthophoto but a poor splat from oblique viewpoints.

Requires RTK fix on drone and XGRIDS scanner, so it is incompatible with BLK2GO data; shows the bridging-tower capture pattern.
